text: I’ll model the requested air volume directly in metres, with flow along +X: inlet at \(x=-40\) mm, a 20 mm core from \(x=0\) to \(20\) mm, and outlet at \(x=100\) mm. I interpret the 8 mm cell width as the clear opening across flats; adjacent cell centres are therefore spaced to leave a 1 mm minimum web. The lattice will be centred on the duct and clipped at the 80 mm square perimeter, which creates partial edge cells as a cut honeycomb core would. I’ll first construct and inspect a coarse CAD representation, then use a conformal volume mesh rather than trying to resolve the 1 mm walls with snappyHexMesh.

The lattice count includes a generous halo; only openings intersecting the square core will survive. I’ll now verify the build123d primitive and transformation signatures before committing the boolean construction.

I noticed the preliminary centre list was offset by the arbitrary halo start rather than exactly centred. I’ll correct it to an integer triangular lattice containing a cell at the duct centre, and test one hexagonal prism’s orientation and dimensions before arraying it.

That test caught an orientation error: the reported 9.238 mm was the corner-to-corner span, not the 8 mm across-flats dimension. Rotating the seed hexagon by 0° places an actual pair of flats across Y; its apothem remains 4 mm in every flat-normal direction. I’ll now build the clipped core solid as an 80 mm square plate minus the array of through-prisms.

The exact core boolean is healthy and contains 105 full or perimeter-clipped passages. Next I’ll subtract that solid from the full square duct, produce a low-resolution surface preview, and inspect both the exterior and a cutaway view before meshing.

The cutaway confirms one connected air volume and the honeycomb plane at the intended core location; the long diagonal lines are only coarse STL triangulation of large planar duct faces. I’ll now inspect the patch exporter, then classify CAD faces by the exact construction planes (not by the shape bounding box): inlet/outlet on their authored X planes, duct walls on the four authored square-wall planes, and every remaining boundary face as honeycomb wall.

The exporter requires a complete, non-overlapping face partition. I’ll apply that exact-plane classification, print face counts and areas for review, and export all four named patches in one welded tessellation.

The patch areas and extents are correct, but the welded surface unexpectedly reports 40 open edges. A fluid solid should be closed, so I will not waive that. I’ll locate those edges and check CAD validity; this is likely a perimeter-cell tangency or tessellation degeneracy that needs correction before meshing.

The CAD kernel reports a valid closed solid, and an independent weld at \(10^{-7}\) m finds zero boundary edges. The exporter’s 40-edge count is therefore a serialization-level mismatch (well below the 0.1 mm tessellation tolerance), not an open CAD shell. I’ll test ASCII STL output, which preserves shared decimal coordinates consistently across patch files, before setting up the coarse background mesh.

I’ll use a 4 mm Cartesian background mesh padded 4 mm outside the closed air surface. snappyHexMesh will retain the internal air region, refine duct boundaries to 2 mm and honeycomb boundaries to 1 mm, and snap conformally to the exact planar honeycomb geometry. This is the coarse-first mesh; no boundary-condition files are being created.
The dictionaries are in place. I’ll generate and inspect only the coarse background grid first; once its dimensions are confirmed, I’ll run the surface-conforming stage.
OpenFOAM requires a minimal case-level `controlDict` even for meshing utilities. I’ll add that administrative dictionary (still no solver or field conditions) and rerun the background mesh.
The background grid is exactly 4 mm and encloses the intended 140×80×80 mm air surface with one-cell padding. I’ll now run snappyHexMesh in-place and review its termination and final cell count.
This OpenFOAM build also insists on empty numerical-scheme dictionaries during mesh creation. I’ll add minimal valid dictionaries only—no equations or boundary conditions—and rerun snappy.
The parser expects named scheme sections even though snappy solves no flow equations. I’ll provide standard empty/default sections and rerun.
The mesher now reads the geometry and only requests two explicit empty optional sections. I’ll add `features` and `refinementRegions`, then continue.
snappy completed with 149,216 cells and no quality-control errors. I’ll now run the binding bare `checkMesh` and inspect patch topology, connectivity, and reported dimensions.

The mesh is one connected region with all four patches and correct extents, but bare `checkMesh` fails on 281 highly skew boundary faces (maximum 8.38). snappy’s default boundary-skew allowance was 20, looser than the binding check. I’ll tighten boundary skewness to 4, rebuild from the background grid, and let snapping back off locally where needed.
The tightened rebuild completed with no skewness violations during snapping. I’ll rerun bare `checkMesh` to verify the final written mesh, since that is the binding result.
Only four faces remain at 4.00017, a numerical hair above `checkMesh`’s limit of 4. Tightening the mesher target to 3.8 provides margin; I’ll rebuild once more from the same background mesh.

The final snap now has explicit margin below the binding skewness threshold. I’ll run `checkMesh` again and, if it passes, render a longitudinal mesh slice to verify that the 1 mm core refinement and open channels are actually present.

Bare `checkMesh` now passes: one region, 149,216 cells, maximum non-orthogonality 58.16°, maximum skewness 3.797, and all four patches form one closed boundary. I’ll make the requested final visual inspection from the actual OpenFOAM mesh, showing a centre-plane slice through the duct and core.

The actual mesh slice shows the 1 mm refined bands along every honeycomb wall, open passages through the full 20 mm core, and smooth coarsening into the upstream/downstream duct. I’ll save the fluid CAD as STEP and numerically verify the final mesh patch planes and core-wall X span from the converted boundary mesh.

Final verification matches the request: inlet at −40 mm, outlet at +100 mm, 80×80 mm section, honeycomb walls spanning nominally 0–20 mm (snapped mesh deviation ±0.052 mm), 8 mm clear across flats, and 1 mm webs. The CAD is a valid closed solid and the final mesh boundary is closed; I am pre-waiving the STL union’s reported 40 exact-coordinate free edges because an independent \(10^{-7}\) m weld gives zero free edges and `checkMesh` confirms a closed singly connected boundary. This is a sub-tessellation serialization mismatch, not an intentional opening.

The union checker independently confirms closure, so the conservative pre-waiver was unnecessary. The remaining coverage notice states that all 2,772 triangles belong to exactly one of the four requested patches; that is the intended complete, non-overlapping partition and is therefore accepted.
